topics.title: Adult CPR and AED
topics.guidanceSource: Resuscitation Council UK — Adult Basic Life Support Guidelines (2025)
steps: If an adult is unresponsive, call emergency services on speaker and check breathing.
If breathing is absent or abnormal, start chest compressions at 100–120 per minute, 5–6 cm deep.
If trained, alternate 30 compressions with 2 breaths. Otherwise keep compressing.
Use an AED as soon as available and follow its prompts.

scenarios.title: Adult collapsed or only gasping
scenarios.summary: An adult is unresponsive and is not breathing normally. Occasional gasps do not count as normal breathing.
scenarios.urgency: Call emergency services and start CPR
steps: Check for danger. Tap the shoulders and shout to check for a response.
If unresponsive, call local emergency services on speaker. Send a helper for an AED (automated external defibrillator).
Open the airway with a head tilt and chin lift. Check breathing for no more than 10 seconds while the call connects. Treat gasping as abnormal.
If breathing is absent or abnormal, begin compressions. Stack your hands on the lower half of the breastbone, with straight arms and shoulders above your hands.
Push 5–6 cm deep at 100–120 compressions/minute. Release pressure fully between pushes. Minimize pauses.
If untrained or unable to give breaths, keep compressing. Follow the dispatcher and use an AED when available.
Continue until rescuers take over, normal breathing and signs of life return, or you cannot continue. Swap with a helper when possible.
avoid: Do not delay CPR to check for a pulse.
Do not mistake gasping for normal breathing.
scenarios.referenceName: Resuscitation Council UK — Adult Basic Life Support (2025)

scenarios.title: CPR with rescue breaths
scenarios.summary: For a trained rescuer helping an adult who is unresponsive and not breathing normally.
scenarios.urgency: 30 compressions, then 2 breaths
steps: Make sure emergency help has been called. Give 30 chest compressions at 100–120 per minute, 5–6 cm deep.
Tilt the head back and lift the chin. Pinch the nose and seal your mouth over theirs.
Give 2 breaths, each lasting about 1 second, with just enough air to raise the chest. Let the chest fall between breaths.
If the first breath fails to raise the chest, adjust the head position and seal before the second attempt. Resume compressions after two attempts.
Repeat 30 compressions and 2 breaths. Keep breathing pauses under 10 seconds. If unable to give breaths, continue chest compressions.
Use an AED when available. Continue until rescuers take over, normal breathing and signs of life return, or you cannot continue.
avoid: Do not blow forcefully or give repeated extra breaths.
Do not delay compressions if breaths cannot be given.
scenarios.referenceName: American Red Cross — Adult CPR Steps

scenarios.title: An AED is available
scenarios.summary: Use an AED alongside CPR for an unresponsive adult who is not breathing normally.
scenarios.urgency: Turn it on and follow the prompts
steps: Ask a helper to prepare the AED while you continue CPR. Turn it on and follow its spoken or visual instructions.
Expose the chest and wipe it dry. Attach the pads to bare skin as pictured: upper right chest and lower left chest below the armpit.
Connect the pads if the device requires it. Keep CPR going while a helper attaches them.
When the AED asks to analyze the heart rhythm, make sure nobody touches the person.
If a shock is advised, check everyone is clear. Press the shock button if instructed; some AEDs deliver the shock automatically.
Immediately restart compressions after a shock or a no-shock message. Leave the pads attached and keep following the AED prompts.
avoid: Do not touch the person during analysis or a shock.
Do not stop CPR just because the AED says no shock is advised.
scenarios.referenceName: American Red Cross — AED Steps

scenarios.title: Unresponsive but breathing normally
scenarios.summary: The person is unresponsive but has regular, normal breathing, including after CPR.
scenarios.urgency: Keep the airway open and monitor breathing
steps: Call emergency services if this has not been done. If normal breathing has returned, stop compressions and keep checking breathing.
If no spinal injury is suspected, place the near arm out, bring the far hand to the near cheek, bend the far knee, and gently roll them towards you onto their side.
Tilt the head back and lift the chin to keep the airway open. Position the upper leg to support them on their side.
If a spinal injury is suspected, minimize movement and follow the dispatcher. If the airway cannot stay open, turn them onto their side, keeping head and spine aligned as far as possible.
Stay with them. If breathing stops or becomes abnormal, including only gasping, roll onto their back and restart CPR.
avoid: Do not use the recovery position for someone who is only gasping.
Do not leave the person alone; keep watching their breathing.
scenarios.referenceName: St John Ambulance — Recovery Position (reviewed April 2025)

topics.title: Falls and Injury
topics.guidanceSource: U.S. National Park Service Outdoor Emergency Plan
steps: Make sure the area is safe. Do not move the person if a head, neck, back, hip, or serious leg injury is possible unless there is immediate danger.
Check responsiveness and breathing. Use SOS or call emergency services immediately for unconsciousness, breathing trouble, severe pain, major bleeding, or an obvious deformity.
For a small wound, rinse away visible dirt with clean water and cover it. For significant bleeding, apply firm, continuous pressure with clean gauze or cloth.
Support a suspected fracture in the position found. Do not straighten it or push exposed bone back in.
Keep the person warm and still, monitor breathing and alertness, and wait for professional rescue if walking could worsen the injury.

scenarios.title: Minor fall or bruise
scenarios.summary: The person is alert, can move normally, and has only mild pain, swelling, or bruising.
scenarios.urgency: Stop, check the whole body, then reassess
steps: Make sure the landing area is safe, then ask the person to stay still briefly while you check what happened and where it hurts.
Check for head impact, neck or back pain, unusual drowsiness, severe pain, deformity, numbness, bleeding, or difficulty breathing before helping them move.
If none of those warning signs are present, help them sit up slowly. Stop if movement causes dizziness, sharp pain, weakness, or nausea.
For a bruise or mild swelling, wrap a cold pack in cloth and apply it for up to 20 minutes. Protect the area from further impact.
Do not resume the hike until walking, balance, and joint movement are comfortable. Arrange assessment if pain or swelling increases.
avoid: Do not immediately pull the person upright after a fall.
Do not continue hiking through worsening pain, dizziness, or reduced movement.
scenarios.referenceName: American Red Cross — Muscle, Bone and Joint Injury

scenarios.title: Suspected fracture
scenarios.summary: There is severe pain, swelling, deformity, grating, inability to use the limb, or bone is visible.
scenarios.urgency: Keep it still and arrange medical help
steps: Use SOS or call 999 for an open fracture, a deformed limb, a cold or numb extremity, severe pain, or a suspected fracture of the neck, back, pelvis, hip, or thigh.
Ask the person to keep still. Support the injured part in the position found by holding above and below the injury.
Remove rings, watches, or tight items early if this can be done without moving the injury, because swelling may increase.
If there is a wound, cover it with a sterile dressing or clean non-fluffy cloth. Press around exposed bone, never directly on it.
Pad around the injury for support, keep the person warm, and repeatedly check colour, warmth, feeling, and circulation beyond the injury.
avoid: Do not straighten the limb or push exposed bone back in.
Do not move the person until the injury is supported unless there is immediate danger.
scenarios.referenceName: St John Ambulance — Broken bones and fractures

scenarios.title: Head injury or concussion
scenarios.summary: The head was struck or jolted, with possible headache, dizziness, confusion, vomiting, or altered behaviour.
scenarios.urgency: Monitor closely; red flags need 999
steps: Tell the person to stop moving and check responsiveness, breathing, neck pain, memory, speech, balance, vision, and limb strength.
Use SOS or call 999 for loss of consciousness, increasing drowsiness, seizure, repeated vomiting, weakness, balance or speech problems, fluid or blood from the ears or nose, or a dangerous fall.
If a neck injury is possible, keep the head and neck still in the position found. Move them only for immediate safety, CPR, or airway care.
For a minor bump without emergency signs, rest and apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth for short periods. The person must not continue hiking alone.
Arrange medical advice and have a responsible adult observe the person for at least 24 hours because symptoms can appear later.
avoid: Do not allow a return to hiking, driving, alcohol, or risky activity while symptoms remain.
Do not leave the person alone or dismiss new confusion, sleepiness, or vomiting.
scenarios.referenceName: NHS — Head injury and concussion

scenarios.title: Neck, back or spinal injury
scenarios.summary: A hard fall, neck or back pain, tingling, numbness, weakness, or loss of movement suggests spinal injury.
scenarios.urgency: Use SOS or call 999 immediately
steps: Tell the person not to move and use SOS or call 999. Share the fall mechanism, exact location, symptoms, and terrain access.
Keep the head, neck, and body in the position found. Ask them to answer verbally rather than nodding or turning.
Support the head on both sides with your hands or rolled clothing only if this can be done without changing its position.
Monitor breathing and responsiveness continuously. If they vomit or the airway becomes blocked, follow emergency-dispatcher instructions and use enough help to keep the spine aligned.
Protect them from cold, rain, and heat while waiting for rescuers, without placing bulky material beneath or moving the spine.
avoid: Do not sit them up, remove a helmet, test movement, or let them walk.
Do not move them except for immediate danger, airway care, or CPR.
scenarios.referenceName: St John Ambulance — Spinal injury first aid

scenarios.title: Dislocated joint
scenarios.summary: A joint looks out of position or deformed and is painful, swollen, or impossible to move normally.
scenarios.urgency: Support it as found and seek urgent care
steps: Stop movement and check for severe bleeding, numbness, pale or cold skin, and whether the injury also involves the head, neck, spine, pelvis, or upper leg.
Arrange urgent medical assessment. Use SOS or call 999 if circulation is reduced, pain is severe, the person cannot be moved safely, or other major injuries are possible.
Support the joint in the most comfortable position found using hands, clothing, padding, or a sling.
Apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth near the joint for up to 20 minutes without pressing or forcing its position.
Recheck warmth, colour, feeling, and circulation beyond the joint while waiting for help.
avoid: Do not attempt to push or pull the joint back into place.
Do not force movement or let the person use the injured joint.
scenarios.referenceName: American Red Cross — Muscle, Bone and Joint Injury

scenarios.title: Major fall or multiple injuries
scenarios.summary: A fall from height, tumbling down a slope, or a hard impact may cause several hidden injuries.
scenarios.urgency: Use SOS or call 999 immediately
steps: Do not rush into unstable terrain. Make the area safe, prevent another fall, and use SOS or call 999 with the exact location and access conditions.
Ask the person not to move. Check responsiveness, breathing, and life-threatening bleeding without twisting the head, neck, or body.
Control life-threatening bleeding with firm direct pressure while keeping a suspected neck or spinal injury as still as possible.
Do not search for every injury by moving limbs. Note pain, deformity, swelling, numbness, breathing difficulty, and changes in alertness for rescuers.
Keep the person warm and continuously monitor breathing and responsiveness. Follow emergency-dispatcher instructions until rescue arrives.
avoid: Do not help the person walk out after a high-energy fall.
Do not give food or drink when emergency treatment may be required.
scenarios.referenceName: American Red Cross — Muscle, Bone and Joint Injury

topics.title: Bleeding
topics.guidanceSource: Malaysian Medical Gazette: First Aid & Basic Life Support
steps: Make sure the scene is safe, then use SOS or call emergency services for bleeding that is spurting, pooling, or will not stop.
Expose the wound and apply firm, continuous direct pressure with clean gauze or cloth. Keep pressing without repeatedly lifting it to check.
If the wound is deep and you are trained, pack it firmly with gauze and continue direct pressure.
For life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg that direct pressure cannot control, apply a commercial tourniquet above the wound, not over a joint, and note the time. Do not loosen it.
Do not remove soaked dressings; add more on top. Keep the person warm and still, and monitor breathing until help arrives.

scenarios.title: Bleeding wound
scenarios.summary: A visible wound that is bleeding but is not spurting or rapidly pooling.
scenarios.urgency: Control the bleeding and reassess
steps: Make sure the area is safe. Use gloves, a plastic bag, or another barrier if one is immediately available.
Check whether anything is embedded. If the wound is clear, press firmly and continuously with clean gauze or cloth.
Keep steady pressure without repeatedly lifting the dressing to check. If blood comes through, keep the first dressing in place and reinforce it while maintaining pressure.
When bleeding is controlled, secure the dressing and check the skin beyond it for normal colour, warmth, and feeling.
Keep the person warm and still. Use SOS or call 999 if bleeding becomes heavy, restarts, or cannot be controlled.
avoid: Do not clean a heavily bleeding wound before the bleeding is controlled.
Do not remove an embedded object.
scenarios.referenceName: Malaysian Medical Gazette — First Aid & Basic Life Support

scenarios.title: Life-threatening bleeding
scenarios.summary: Blood is continuously flowing, spurting, rapidly pooling, or the person shows signs of shock.
scenarios.urgency: Use SOS or call 999 immediately
steps: Call for emergency help immediately and expose the wound so the bleeding source is visible.
Place clean gauze, cloth, or a haemostatic dressing directly on the wound and apply firm, continuous pressure.
Keep pressing until bleeding stops, another person relieves you, or a tourniquet is ready for life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg.
If trained and a commercial tourniquet is available, place it 5–7 cm above the wound, never over the wound or a joint. Tighten until bleeding stops, note the time, and do not loosen it.
Keep the person warm, still, and reassured. Continually watch breathing and responsiveness until help arrives.
avoid: Do not delay direct pressure while searching for perfect equipment.
Do not loosen or remove a tourniquet after it has controlled life-threatening bleeding.
scenarios.referenceName: American Red Cross — Life-Threatening External Bleeding

scenarios.title: Object embedded in wound
scenarios.summary: Glass, a branch, metal, or another object remains lodged in the wound.
scenarios.urgency: Stabilise it and get urgent medical help
steps: Use SOS or call 999 for a large, deep, or dangerously positioned embedded object.
Do not remove the object. It may be limiting blood loss and removal can worsen the injury.
Apply firm pressure on either side of the object, never directly on top of it.
Build padding around the object with clean dressings, then bandage around the padding to hold it steady without pushing it deeper.
Keep the person still, monitor circulation beyond the injury, and watch for shock while waiting for help.
avoid: Do not pull, twist, shorten, or press down on the object.
Do not give food or drink if emergency treatment may be required.
scenarios.referenceName: St John Ambulance — Severe bleeding first aid

scenarios.title: Nosebleed
scenarios.summary: Bleeding is coming from one or both nostrils without another major wound.
scenarios.urgency: Pinch continuously for 10–15 minutes
steps: Sit upright and lean forward with the mouth open. Do not tilt the head back.
Pinch the soft part of the nose just above the nostrils and hold continuously for 10–15 minutes. Time it without releasing to check.
Breathe through the mouth and spit out blood rather than swallowing it.
Use 999 or urgent medical care if bleeding is excessive, lasts beyond 10–15 minutes, follows a blow to the head, causes weakness or dizziness, or makes breathing difficult.
After it stops, avoid blowing or picking the nose, hot drinks, alcohol, heavy lifting, and strenuous exercise for 24 hours.
avoid: Do not lean back or lie flat.
Do not stuff tissue or cotton wool into the nose.
scenarios.referenceName: NHS — Nosebleed

scenarios.title: Minor cut or graze
scenarios.summary: A shallow wound with light bleeding that stops with brief pressure.
scenarios.urgency: Clean and protect once bleeding stops
steps: Wash and dry your hands, and put on disposable gloves if available.
Apply gentle pressure with clean gauze or cloth until bleeding stops.
Rinse the wound with clean bottled or tap water. Clean the surrounding skin with soap and water, wiping away from the wound.
Pat dry and cover with a sterile dressing or plaster. Keep it clean and dry and change it when wet or dirty.
Seek medical advice for a dirty wound that will not clean, a bite, increasing redness or pain, pus, fever, loss of feeling, or a large or deep cut.
avoid: Do not put unverified creams, powders, leaves, or soil into the wound.
Do not continue hiking if the wound keeps reopening or function is affected.
scenarios.referenceName: NHS — Cuts and grazes

scenarios.title: Suspected internal bleeding
scenarios.summary: After a fall or impact: pain, swelling, rigid abdomen, unusual bruising, blood in vomit or urine, or signs of shock.
scenarios.urgency: Use SOS or call 999 immediately
steps: Treat suspected internal bleeding as an emergency and share the exact location and injury mechanism with responders.
Keep the person in the position found if a head, neck, or back injury is possible, unless movement is required for immediate safety or CPR.
If shock is suspected and no spinal injury is likely, let the person lie flat or use the position most comfortable for breathing.
Keep them warm without overheating, reassure them, and continuously monitor breathing and responsiveness.
Do not give anything to eat or drink. Be ready to begin CPR if they become unresponsive and are not breathing normally.
avoid: Do not assume there is no serious bleeding because no blood is visible.
Do not let the person walk out or continue hiking.
scenarios.referenceName: American Red Cross — Life-Threatening Internal Bleeding

topics.title: Sprain or Twisted Ankle
steps: Stop hiking and protect the joint from further movement. Do not force weight onto the injured ankle.
Wrap ice or a cold pack in cloth and apply it for up to 20 minutes at a time. Never place ice directly on skin.
Use a supportive elastic bandage if available, firm but not tight. Loosen it if toes become numb, cold, pale, or more painful.
Raise the ankle at or above heart level when practical and rest it for the next several days.
Seek urgent medical assessment for severe pain, deformity, numbness, a cold foot, a popping sound with loss of function, or inability to walk.

scenarios.title: Mild ankle sprain
scenarios.summary: The ankle is painful or mildly swollen, but has no deformity and limited gentle weight-bearing is possible.
scenarios.urgency: Protect it and stop hiking for now
steps: Stop and sit somewhere safe. Remove the pack and protect the ankle from further twisting or impact.
Rest the ankle and avoid weight-bearing that causes pain. Use trekking poles or assistance only to reach immediate safety.
Wrap a cold pack in cloth and apply it for up to 20 minutes. Wait at least 20 minutes before repeating.
Apply an elastic support if available, starting at the foot and wrapping upward. It should feel supportive, never tight.
Elevate the ankle when practical and arrange a safe return. Resume normal movement gradually only when pain no longer stops it.
avoid: Do not apply ice directly to skin.
Avoid heat, alcohol, massage, and strenuous activity during the first two to three days.
scenarios.referenceName: NHS — Sprains and strains

scenarios.title: Cannot bear weight or heard a pop
scenarios.summary: Severe pain, rapid swelling, a pop or snap, or inability to walk may indicate a major sprain or fracture.
scenarios.urgency: Treat as a possible fracture
steps: Stop movement and do not ask the person to test the ankle again.
Use SOS or arrange urgent assessment if they cannot walk more than a few steps, pain is severe, or swelling is rapidly increasing.
Support the ankle in the position found with padding, clothing, or a splint only if trained. Do not straighten it.
Apply a wrapped cold pack for no more than 20 minutes if the wound is closed and this does not delay evacuation.
Keep the person warm and monitor pain, swelling, colour, warmth, feeling, and movement of the toes until help arrives.
avoid: Do not force the person to walk out on the injured ankle.
Do not attempt to straighten a deformed ankle.
scenarios.referenceName: American Red Cross — Muscle, Bone and Joint Injury

scenarios.title: Deformity or open wound
scenarios.summary: The ankle looks bent or displaced, bone may be visible, or there is a wound over the suspected fracture.
scenarios.urgency: Use SOS or call 999 immediately
steps: Call 999 or use SOS and keep the person still. Share the precise location and terrain access.
Control bleeding with a sterile dressing or clean cloth, pressing around—not on—exposed bone or the deformity.
Support the limb above and below the injury in the position found. Add padding without forcing alignment.
Remove rings, anklets, or tight footwear only if this can be done without moving the injury.
Monitor breathing and shock, keep the person warm, and recheck circulation beyond the injury while awaiting rescue.
avoid: Do not push exposed bone back in or reposition the joint.
Do not give food or drink when emergency treatment may be needed.
scenarios.referenceName: St John Ambulance — Broken bones and fractures

scenarios.title: Foot becomes numb, pale or cold
scenarios.summary: Reduced feeling, unusual colour, cold skin, or worsening pain can mean impaired circulation or excessive compression.
scenarios.urgency: Loosen compression and get urgent help
steps: Stop and compare both feet for colour, warmth, feeling, and toe movement.
If an elastic wrap was applied, loosen or remove it while keeping the injured ankle supported.
Use SOS or call 999 if normal colour, warmth, and feeling do not return promptly or the injury is deformed.
Keep the ankle still in the position found and protect it from pressure, cold, and further movement.
Repeat circulation checks while waiting for professional help and report any worsening numbness or pain.
avoid: Do not tighten a bandage to control swelling.
Do not continue hiking on a numb, pale, blue, or cold foot.
scenarios.referenceName: American Red Cross — Muscle, Bone and Joint Injury

topics.title: Heat Exhaustion
steps: Stop hiking and move the person to shade, air conditioning, or the coolest available place.
Loosen or remove unnecessary clothing. Cool the skin with wet cloths, water, fanning, and cold packs at the neck and armpits.
Give small, frequent sips of cool water or an electrolyte drink only if the person is fully alert and not vomiting.
Do not leave the person alone. Arrange medical help if symptoms worsen, vomiting occurs, or recovery is not prompt.
Confusion, fainting, seizures, or very hot skin may mean heat stroke: call emergency services immediately, cool rapidly, and do not give anything by mouth if alertness is impaired.

scenarios.title: Heat cramps
scenarios.summary: Painful muscle cramps or spasms occur during heavy sweating, usually in the legs, arms, or abdomen.
scenarios.urgency: Stop activity and replace fluids
steps: Stop hiking and move to shade or the coolest available place.
Sit or lie down, loosen unnecessary clothing, and gently rest the cramped muscles.
If fully alert and not vomiting, drink water plus an electrolyte or carbohydrate drink in small amounts every 15 to 20 minutes.
Do not resume strenuous activity for several hours after the cramps settle; arrange a safe return instead.
Seek medical help if cramps last more than one hour, recur, or the person has heart problems or follows a low-sodium diet.
avoid: Do not use salt tablets.
Do not treat cramps as harmless if weakness, dizziness, confusion, or vomiting develops.
scenarios.referenceName: CDC/NIOSH — Heat-related illnesses

scenarios.title: Heat exhaustion
scenarios.summary: Heavy sweating, headache, nausea, dizziness, thirst, weakness, irritability, or reduced urine suggests heat exhaustion.
scenarios.urgency: Cool now and arrange medical assessment
steps: Stop hiking and move the person into shade, air conditioning, or the coolest available place.
Remove the pack, shoes, socks, and unnecessary or tight clothing.
Cool the head, face, neck, and skin with cool water, wet cloths, cold compresses, and fanning.
If fully alert and not vomiting, give frequent small sips of cool water or an electrolyte drink.
Do not leave them alone. Seek medical assessment; call 999 if symptoms worsen, vomiting prevents drinking, confusion develops, or recovery is not prompt.
avoid: Do not allow the person to continue hiking after temporary improvement.
Do not give fluids if alertness is impaired or swallowing is unsafe.
scenarios.referenceName: KKM InfoSihat — Cuaca Panas

scenarios.title: Dizzy or fainted in heat
scenarios.summary: Brief fainting, dizziness, or light-headedness can follow heat exposure, dehydration, or standing suddenly.
scenarios.urgency: Lie down, cool, and reassess
steps: Prevent a fall and help the person lie down in a cool, shaded place.
Check responsiveness and normal breathing. If unresponsive or not breathing normally, call 999 and begin appropriate emergency care.
Loosen clothing and cool them with water, wet cloths, and fanning.
Once fully alert and able to swallow, offer small sips of water, clear juice, or an electrolyte drink.
Arrange medical assessment if fainting was prolonged, happened during exertion, recurs, caused injury, or is accompanied by chest pain, confusion, or breathing difficulty.
avoid: Do not make the person stand up quickly.
Do not assume every faint in hot weather is harmless.
scenarios.referenceName: CDC/NIOSH — Heat syncope

scenarios.title: Heat stroke warning signs
scenarios.summary: Confusion, slurred speech, seizure, collapse, very hot skin, or loss of consciousness indicates a life-threatening emergency.
scenarios.urgency: Call 999 and cool immediately
steps: Use SOS or call 999 immediately. Heat stroke can cause death or permanent disability if treatment is delayed.
Move the person to shade or the coolest available place and remove outer clothing and equipment.
Cool rapidly: immerse in cool or ice water if safely possible, or soak the skin and clothing with cool water while fanning continuously.
Place cold wet cloths or wrapped ice packs at the head, neck, armpits, and groin while awaiting emergency help.
Continuously monitor breathing and responsiveness. Begin CPR if they become unresponsive and are not breathing normally.
avoid: Do not delay cooling while waiting for transport.
Do not give anything by mouth when the person is confused, drowsy, vomiting, or unconscious.
scenarios.referenceName: CDC/NIOSH — Heat stroke first aid

scenarios.title: Severe muscle pain or dark urine
scenarios.summary: Unusual muscle pain, marked weakness, or tea- or cola-coloured urine after heat and exertion may indicate muscle breakdown.
scenarios.urgency: Stop activity and seek immediate care
steps: Stop hiking immediately and move to a cool place.
Use SOS or arrange urgent medical transport; tell responders about the heat exposure, exertion, muscle symptoms, and urine colour.
Rest the affected muscles and remove unnecessary clothing or equipment.
If fully alert and not vomiting, give water in small amounts while awaiting professional instructions.
Monitor for confusion, collapse, abnormal heartbeat, seizure, or reduced urine, and call 999 if any occur.
avoid: Do not massage painful muscles or continue exercising.
Do not wait for the urine colour to return to normal before seeking care.
scenarios.referenceName: CDC/NIOSH — Rhabdomyolysis associated with heat

topics.title: Snake Bite
steps: Move away from the snake. Do not approach, catch, or kill it. Take a photo only from a safe distance if this causes no delay.
Treat every snake bite as an emergency: use SOS or call emergency services and arrange urgent transport. Do not drive yourself.
Keep the person calm and as still as possible, seated or lying down, with the bitten limb in a neutral, comfortable position.
Remove rings, watches, and tight clothing before swelling starts. Wash gently with soap and water if available and cover with a clean, dry dressing.
Mark the leading edge of swelling and write the time. Do not use ice, a tourniquet, electric shock, alcohol, cutting, suction, or folk remedies.

scenarios.title: Bite with no symptoms yet
scenarios.summary: Fang marks may be small and serious effects can be delayed, even when pain or swelling is absent.
scenarios.urgency: Treat every suspected bite as an emergency
steps: Move everyone away from the snake without approaching, trapping, or killing it.
Use SOS or call 999 immediately and arrange transport to a hospital. Do not wait for symptoms to appear.
Keep the person calm, lying or seated, and completely still. Carry them rather than allowing them to walk when possible.
Remove rings, watches, footwear, and tight clothing from the bitten limb before swelling begins.
Note the bite time and location. Photograph the snake only from a safe distance if this causes no delay or additional risk.
avoid: Do not cut, suck, burn, massage, or apply herbs to the bite.
Do not apply ice, electric shock, or a tight tourniquet.
scenarios.referenceName: Ministry of Health Malaysia — Guideline Management of Snakebite

scenarios.title: Swelling or pain is spreading
scenarios.summary: Increasing swelling, tenderness, bruising, blistering, or bleeding can indicate progressing envenomation.
scenarios.urgency: Immobilise and transport urgently
steps: Confirm that emergency help and hospital transport are already being arranged.
Keep the person and bitten limb as still as possible in a neutral, comfortable position.
Remove constricting items and loosely cover the bite with a clean, dry dressing.
Mark the leading edge of swelling on the skin and write the time beside it; repeat only if swelling advances.
Monitor breathing, alertness, bleeding, swelling, and circulation while keeping the person reassured and still.
avoid: Do not tightly wrap the limb unless specifically directed by Malaysian medical professionals trained for the identified snake.
Do not give aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen, alcohol, or folk remedies.
scenarios.referenceName: CDC/NIOSH — Venomous snakes

scenarios.title: Drooping, weakness or breathing trouble
scenarios.summary: Drooping eyelids, blurred vision, difficulty speaking or swallowing, weakness, or breathing difficulty may indicate neurotoxic venom.
scenarios.urgency: Call 999; airway support may be needed
steps: Call 999 immediately or update responders that breathing or neurological symptoms have developed.
Keep the person lying still and continuously observe breathing, speech, swallowing, and alertness.
Loosen clothing around the neck and chest while maintaining warmth and privacy.
If vomiting occurs and the airway cannot be protected, place the person on their side while minimising movement.
If they become unresponsive and are not breathing normally, begin CPR and follow emergency-dispatcher instructions.
avoid: Do not give food, drink, or oral medicine when swallowing is difficult or alertness is impaired.
Do not transport them walking, riding alone, or driving themselves.
scenarios.referenceName: World Health Organization — Snakebite

scenarios.title: Collapsed or unconscious
scenarios.summary: Collapse, seizure, severe bleeding, shock, or unconsciousness after a bite is immediately life-threatening.
scenarios.urgency: Use SOS or call 999 immediately
steps: Ensure 999 has been called and make the location accessible to rescuers if this can be done safely.
Check responsiveness and normal breathing while keeping the person as still as possible.
If breathing normally, protect the airway in a side position while minimising movement of the bitten limb.
If not breathing normally, begin CPR and use an AED if available, following its prompts.
Keep monitoring and be ready to report the bite time, symptoms, snake appearance, and any first aid already given.
avoid: Do not delay resuscitation to photograph or identify the snake.
Tell responders immediately if a tight tourniquet was applied, and follow their instructions before altering it.
scenarios.referenceName: World Health Organization — Snakebite envenoming first aid

topics.title: Lost or Stranded
topics.guidanceSource: U.S. National Park Service Hike Smart
steps: Stop. Think, observe, and make a calm plan. Stay near the trail or your last known position unless remaining there creates immediate danger.
Use SOS or contact emergency services and share the app's exact location pin, route, condition, clothing, supplies, and number of people.
Preserve phone power: enable low-power mode, dim the screen, close unnecessary apps, and avoid repeated calls. Keep communication available for rescuers.
Protect the group from rain, wind, cold, heat, and darkness. Use available shelter, clothing, food, and water carefully.
Signal in groups of three with a whistle, light, or visible material. Once rescuers know your position, remain there unless they instruct otherwise.

scenarios.title: Recently off route
scenarios.summary: You have just lost the marked trail but still know your recent route or last confirmed point.
scenarios.urgency: Stop before moving farther away
steps: Stop, breathe, and gather the group. Do not let anyone search alone.
Mark or save the current location in HikerCircle and check the recorded route, offline map, compass, and visible landmarks.
Identify the last place where the route was certain. Retrace only if the path back is clearly safe and confidently recognised.
If the route cannot be confirmed quickly, stop self-rescue, contact help, and remain at a safe fixed location.
Tell a trusted contact or rescuers the current coordinates, last known trail point, group size, clothing colours, supplies, and conditions.
avoid: Do not follow an unfamiliar river, drainage, shortcut, or steep slope.
Do not keep walking merely to feel that progress is being made.
scenarios.referenceName: U.S. National Park Service — Outdoor Emergency Plan

scenarios.title: No signal or low battery
scenarios.summary: Phone service is unreliable or the remaining battery must be preserved for location and rescue contact.
scenarios.urgency: Conserve power and establish a visible position
steps: Stay at a safe, identifiable location and record the coordinates, time, and nearby landmarks while the phone is available.
Enable battery saver, dim the screen, close nonessential apps, and keep the phone warm and dry.
Try emergency contact briefly from the fixed location. Send one concise message containing coordinates, trail, condition, and group size when service appears.
Use a whistle, signal mirror, bright clothing, or flashlight patterns rather than continuous shouting or lighting.
Check for messages or signal at spaced intervals without wandering to exposed ridges or dangerous terrain solely for reception.
avoid: Do not continuously redial, stream media, or leave navigation running at full brightness.
Do not climb unsafe terrain just to obtain phone signal.
scenarios.referenceName: U.S. National Park Service — Outdoor Emergency Plan

scenarios.title: Darkness is approaching
scenarios.summary: Continuing without a clearly recognised trail and reliable lighting may increase fall and navigation risk.
scenarios.urgency: Stop early and prepare to remain safely
steps: Stop before visibility becomes too poor and choose a stable place away from cliffs, rivers, dead branches, and flood channels.
Share or record the exact location and contact emergency services if the group cannot return safely.
Put on warm and rain-protective layers before becoming cold, and insulate the group from wet ground.
Inventory water, food, lighting, first aid, and battery. Ration lighting and phone use, not essential drinking water.
Make the location visible and use recognised distress signals while remaining together until daylight or rescue instructions.
avoid: Do not continue through unfamiliar steep terrain just to avoid an overnight wait.
Do not build a fire where it could spread or violate local restrictions.
scenarios.referenceName: National Park Service — Hike Smart emergency guidance

scenarios.title: Injured and unable to continue
scenarios.summary: An injury, illness, exhaustion, or unsafe terrain prevents the person or group from hiking out.
scenarios.urgency: Use SOS and remain at the reported location
steps: Stabilise immediate threats such as breathing problems, severe bleeding, dangerous heat, or cold.
Use SOS or call 999 and provide coordinates, injury details, number of people, clothing colours, equipment, and route access.
Do not move the injured person if a head, neck, spine, pelvis, hip, or serious leg injury is possible unless there is immediate danger.
Protect the person from rain, wind, ground cold, and direct sun while monitoring breathing and alertness.
Keep the location fixed after reporting it. If someone must seek help, send a capable pair with written location and patient details rather than leaving the person alone.
avoid: Do not attempt a difficult carry without training or enough helpers.
Do not relocate after rescuers have your coordinates unless safety requires it or they instruct you.
scenarios.referenceName: National Park Service — Wilderness safety

scenarios.title: A group member is missing
scenarios.summary: Someone has become separated and their exact location is unknown.
scenarios.urgency: Stop the group and report the last known point
steps: Stop the activity, account for everyone, and gather the remaining group together.
Return together only to the missing person's last confirmed location if that route is known and safe.
Call 999 or use SOS with the last known coordinates, time last seen, intended route, description, clothing, equipment, medical needs, and phone number.
Ask the missing person by message or call to stay put and share their location if contact is established.
Wait at the agreed or last known location when safe, make the group visible, and follow search-and-rescue instructions.
avoid: Do not split into multiple uncoordinated search parties or search off trail.
Do not erase footprints, move abandoned equipment, or change the agreed meeting point without informing rescuers.
scenarios.referenceName: U.S. National Park Service — Outdoor Emergency Plan

topics.title: Severe Weather
topics.guidanceSource: U.S. National Weather Service Lightning Safety
steps: Turn back early when warnings, thunder, rapidly rising water, poor visibility, or unsafe footing develop.
For lightning, leave ridges, summits, open ground, water, isolated trees, wire fences, and metal structures. The safest shelter is a substantial building or hard-topped vehicle.
If flash flooding is possible, move to higher ground immediately. Never enter or cross moving floodwater.
Keep the group together while moving to shelter, protect phones and emergency equipment from water, and share your location and revised plan.
Wait at least 30 minutes after the last thunder before leaving lightning shelter. Use SOS for injury, entrapment, hypothermia, or inability to reach safety.

scenarios.title: Thunder or lightning
scenarios.summary: Every Malaysian thunderstorm can produce dangerous lightning, including before heavy rain reaches the trail.
scenarios.urgency: Leave exposed terrain immediately
steps: Stop the hike when thunder is heard or lightning is seen; do not wait for rain to begin.
Move away from summits, ridges, open ground, water, metal fences, poles, and isolated trees.
Enter a substantial enclosed building or hard-topped vehicle if reachable without crossing exposed terrain.
If no safe structure exists, move to a lower non-flooding area, spread the group apart, and minimise contact with the ground.
Wait at least 30 minutes after the last thunder before resuming. Call 999 and begin CPR or use an AED if someone is struck and is not breathing normally.
avoid: Do not shelter under an isolated tree, open hut, tent, or small rain shelter.
Do not remain in water or on exposed high ground.
scenarios.referenceName: METMalaysia — Thunderstorm and lightning safety

scenarios.title: Rising river or flash flood
scenarios.summary: Rapidly rising, muddy, or fast-moving water can arrive from heavy rain upstream even when local rain is light.
scenarios.urgency: Move to higher ground immediately
steps: Turn away from the water and move to stable higher ground without crossing the flow.
Leave riverbanks, waterfalls, drainage channels, narrow valleys, and low bridges immediately.
Keep the group together and identify a route that continues upward, not along the river.
Use SOS or call 999 if trapped, cut off, injured, or unable to reach safe ground; share the exact location and water conditions.
Remain on high ground and follow official instructions until water clearly recedes and the route is confirmed safe.
avoid: Do not wade, swim, jump, or drive through moving floodwater.
Do not use a submerged, damaged, or unstable bridge.
scenarios.referenceName: METMalaysia — Monsoon and flash-flood preparedness

scenarios.title: Strong wind or falling branches
scenarios.summary: Squalls and thunderstorms can bring sudden strong winds, falling limbs, and unstable trees.
scenarios.urgency: Leave trees, ridges, and exposed edges
steps: Stop and move away from ridgelines, cliff edges, isolated trees, dead branches, and visibly leaning or damaged trees.
Seek a substantial building or hard-topped vehicle when safely reachable.
If no building is available, choose a low stable area away from flood channels and tree-fall hazards.
Secure loose equipment, keep the group low and together, and protect the head and eyes from debris.
Use SOS if anyone is struck, trapped, separated, or unable to move to safer ground.
avoid: Do not shelter in a tent, under a lone tree, or beside a damaged tree.
Do not continue along exposed ridges or suspension bridges during strong gusts.
scenarios.referenceName: METMalaysia — Weather phenomena and thunderstorm hazards

scenarios.title: Cold, soaked or shivering
scenarios.summary: Heavy rain, wind, exhaustion, and wet clothing can cool the body dangerously even in Malaysia.
scenarios.urgency: Stop heat loss and seek shelter
steps: Move out of wind and rain into the driest safe shelter available.
Remove wet outer layers when dry replacements are available, then add insulation around the head, neck, chest, and body.
Insulate the person from wet ground and share shelter or body warmth without rubbing cold skin.
If fully alert and able to swallow, offer a warm sweet non-alcoholic drink and energy food.
Use SOS or call 999 for confusion, clumsiness, slurred speech, worsening drowsiness, stopped shivering, or inability to rewarm.
avoid: Do not use very hot water, direct high heat, alcohol, or vigorous massage.
Do not make a confused or severely cold person walk.
scenarios.referenceName: National Park Service — Hiking weather and hypothermia safety

scenarios.title: Fog or very poor visibility
scenarios.summary: Fog and intense rain can hide trail markers, junctions, cliffs, and other group members.
scenarios.urgency: Slow down; stop if the route is uncertain
steps: Bring the group together immediately and confirm every member is present.
Stop at a safe point away from edges, waterways, and falling-branch hazards if the next trail marker cannot be seen.
Save the current location and compare the recorded route, offline map, compass, and last confirmed trail point.
Retrace only when the route is confidently known and safe; otherwise remain visible and contact help.
Use lights, bright clothing, voices, or whistles to maintain group contact without splitting up.
avoid: Do not shortcut switchbacks or follow an unverified path in poor visibility.
Do not allow faster members to move ahead alone.
scenarios.referenceName: National Park Service — Outdoor Emergency Plan

scenarios.title: Landslide or unstable ground
scenarios.summary: Heavy rain can loosen slopes; cracking sounds, falling rocks, moving soil, or sudden muddy flow require immediate retreat.
scenarios.urgency: Leave the slope and drainage path
steps: Turn around immediately when the trail surface moves, rocks begin falling, or a slope shows fresh cracks or flowing debris.
Move away from the slide path, steep cut slopes, gullies, stream channels, and the base of unstable cliffs.
Choose stable higher ground using an established route without crossing active debris or fast water.
Warn nearby group members without entering the danger area and account for everyone from safety.
Use SOS or call 999 for entrapment, injury, blocked retreat, or a missing member, and report the exact affected location.
avoid: Do not climb over fresh slide debris or stop beneath a damaged slope.
Do not return until authorities or trail managers confirm the route is safe.
scenarios.referenceName: METMalaysia — Heavy rain, flash floods and landslide hazards
